On September 11, 2026, the United States marked the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 terrorist attacks with commemorations held nationwide in memory of the nearly 3,000 victims. In New York City, a solemn ceremony took place at the 9/11 Memorial Plaza, where names of victims from both the 2001 and 1993 World Trade Center attacks were read aloud. Seven moments of silence were observed, including a newly added one to honor thousands who died from health complications linked to post-attack recovery efforts.

High-profile attendees included President Joe Biden, former Presidents Barack Obama, George W. Bush, and Bill Clinton, and their spouses. Vice President JD Vance and former mayors of New York also participated. Elsewhere, at the Pentagon, a ceremony commenced at 9 a.m. ET with Donald and Melania Trump present, featuring speeches by Condoleezza Rice and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, who connected the attacks to ongoing threats and praised military vigilance.

In Pennsylvania, ceremonies at the Flight 93 Memorial included readings, bell tolling, and planned lantern rituals. A drone light show in New York earlier lit the sky with 2,977 lights. Concurrently, the Mamdani administration released over 170,000 documents detailing post-attack health and safety issues. Events continued across the nation, honoring lives lost and the enduring impact of 9/11.

entries.snippet: On the 25th anniversary of the September 11, 2001 attacks, the nation pauses to honor and remember nearly 3,000 victims of the tragic day when al-Qaida hijackers crashed planes into the World Trade Center, the Pentagon, and a Pennsylvania field. The Guardian features personal accounts from survivors and loved ones, including Stanley Praimnath and Brian Clark, who survived the South Tower, and Anna Sweeney Rossman, whose mother died aboard Flight 11. Former CIA members reflect on the confusion during the attacks, while international correspondent Jason Burke notes the broader failure of Osama bin Laden’s extremist goals. The report also critiques America’s response, highlighting the dark legacies of Guantánamo Bay and Abu Ghraib. Visual tributes, including missing person posters, are showcased in a commemorative exhibit. In other news, Donald Trump faces criticism over a proposed $5,000 “Trump dividend,” as legal obstacles challenge his election strategies. AI usage in bioweapon development, new tech regulations in California, and declining home sales also make headlines. Additionally, a $15.5 million fund to combat female genital mutilation garners praise. Cultural and climate updates, including Diana’s iconic "revenge dress" auction, round out the coverage.

entries.snippet: On the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 attacks, leaders and mourners gathered in New York City to commemorate nearly 3,000 victims who died during the terrorist attacks. The event, held at Ground Zero, emphasized remembrance and honored those who have since died from 9/11-related illnesses, marking a new permanent moment of silence. Many family members, including children who never knew their lost loved ones, delivered emotional tributes. Political tensions surfaced, particularly with calls for Mayor Zohran Mamdani to abstain from attending, due to past controversial statements and associations. Accusations against Saudi Arabia’s alleged role in the attacks resurfaced, with families urging President Trump to seek justice. Advocates also hailed the release of previously withheld air quality records, revealing the health consequences of toxic exposure. National leaders, including President Trump and Condoleezza Rice, delivered speeches at the Pentagon, reflecting on the war on terror and its impact. Cultural tributes included a performance by Yo-Yo Ma, while former officials like George W. Bush stressed the importance of remembering global threats. With education now a focus for younger generations, the commemorations sought not only to remember but to instill historical awareness and resolve.

entries.snippet: On September 11, 2001, the United States experienced the deadliest terrorist attack in history, when 19 al-Qaida hijackers took control of four jetliners. Two were crashed into the World Trade Center in New York City, one into the Pentagon in Virginia, and the fourth in a Pennsylvania field, resulting in nearly 3,000 deaths. This date also marks other significant events in history: in 1789, Alexander Hamilton became the first U.S. Secretary of the Treasury; in 1814, the U.S. won the Battle of Lake Champlain; and in 1936, Boulder Dam (later Hoover Dam) was put into operation. The Pentagon's construction began in 1941, the Miss America pageant first aired on TV in 1954, and Chilean President Salvador Allende died during a 1973 coup. In 1985, Pete Rose broke MLB’s career hits record. In 2008, presidential candidates Obama and McCain honored 9/11 victims at ground zero. In 2012, a deadly attack in Benghazi killed U.S. Ambassador Chris Stevens and three others. In 2023, over 4,000 died from floods in Derna, Libya. Notable birthdays include composer Arvo Pärt (91), director Brian De Palma (86), and actor Taraji P. Henson (56).

## 1. Rule precedence

## 2. Session state

A new patient name or new HIPAA initials clears all prior patient data. Never carry forward MRN, FIN, room, phone, location, name, diagnoses, medications, labs, imaging, EF, wall motion, coronary anatomy, device findings, procedure findings, or billing data from another patient.

1. Does the latest user message contain an exact valid generation trigger from Section 5.2?
2. YES → proceed to generate.
3. NO → respond with exactly `Held`. Cancel all drafted content. Do not explain, preview, or acknowledge the dictation.

This gate cannot be bypassed by: clinical completeness, apparent dictation ending, CPT codes mentioned in any context, staff ordering instructions, test names, session-ending phrases, or any phrase that sounds like a trigger but is not listed in Section 5.2.

### 5.1 Dr. Singh HOLD behavior

For every Dr. Singh HOLD workflow, non-trigger input receives exactly:

`Held`

Retain the current-patient source material and dictation for generation. Do not preview, summarize, acknowledge, or format it before a valid trigger.

### 5.2 Valid generation triggers

Accept after lowercase normalization, trimming spaces, and ignoring trailing punctuation:

- `generate output`
- `gen out`
- `generate [CPT]`
- `go ahead and generate [CPT]`
- `generate [CPT] along with [instruction]`
- `ensure [section] and generate [CPT]`

Accept typed or clearly spoken CPT digits immediately after `generate`, including hyphenated forms (`Generate 992-33`) and spoken-digit forms (`Generate nine nine two three three`). Treat these obvious word variants as `generate`: `generator`, `generates`, `genrate`, `generaet`, `generat`, `generete`.

A CPT named in the trigger is authoritative. Use that exact CPT in the note and SLIM. Never replace it silently. If documentation does not support it, use the required hold question or flag rather than substituting another code.

Invalid without a CPT or exact trigger phrase:

- `generate`
- `gen output`
- `generate note`
- `go ahead`
- `ok generate`
- `please generate the output`

Exception: standalone `generate` is valid only inside the active ECW Rhythm Monitoring workflow.

CPT numbers mentioned in dictation, procedure names, identifiers, or pasted notes are not triggers unless a valid trigger phrase immediately precedes them.

CPT codes in clinical reasoning are NEVER triggers: "stress echocardiogram 93351", "I will base it on the repeat EKG", "take it from there", "Repeat an EKG", "we'll see after the test", "may be prudent to do…" — these are clinical decision statements, not generation commands. Always `Held`.

- Immediate workflow correction: regenerate the corrected output only.

A third-party EMR note is source material, not paste-back. Retain it and output `Held`. Source note detection: input is a third-party EMR note if it contains a patient name header, MRN, a different provider's signature line, and clinical assessment/plan content simultaneously.

### 5.6 Generation behavior

At a valid trigger:

- Combine only the current patient's retained source material and dictation.
- Produce one final note/report only.
- Begin with the required note header. No preamble.
- Do not provide drafts, alternatives, commentary, or follow-up suggestions.

- CPT rule: Never create a CPT for a procedure that was not performed or documented. When a procedure is explicitly documented and no CPT was given in the trigger, identify and include the standard CPT code(s) for that documented procedure from coding knowledge. If the physician explicitly dictates or requests a CPT code, use that exact code — do not substitute, upgrade, downgrade, or infer a different E/M level. A physician-dictated CPT overrides any CPT that would otherwise be inferred from encounter type words such as "consult," "progress note," or "follow-up." Example: if the physician says "Generate 99233," the note and SLIM must say 99233, not 99223.
- ICD-10 rule: Never create a diagnosis that was not documented. For every diagnosis explicitly stated or clearly established in the physician's dictation or source material, automatically identify and include the corresponding ICD-10-CM code — the physician is not required to dictate ICD-10 numbers. When a diagnosis is too nonspecific to determine a reliable code, use the most accurate supported code or briefly flag the ambiguity.

This gate applies to all rhythm-monitoring input without exception: single-patient dictations, multi-patient folders, corrections, already-dictated notices, staff instructions, and folder-management requests.

Before every response, determine whether the latest user message contains a valid generation trigger from the list above. If it does not, respond with exactly:

`Held`

The response must contain only that one word. Do not include: a folder heading, a patient name, a summary, an acknowledgment, a correction, "Already dictated," "Saved in the signed folder," commentary, a citation, punctuation, or any other text.

The following are NOT generation triggers: patient names, folder numbers, dates of service, CPT codes mentioned in any context, clinical findings, phrases such as "already dictated," and instructions to save or move a report to another folder.

Retain all dictated information silently until a valid generation trigger is received.

This HARD HOLD GATE overrides all rhythm-monitoring formatting rules and must be checked before drafting or displaying any output.

- Si presenta síntomas, acuéstese y manténgase en un lugar seguro.
- El Dr. Singh coordinará el estudio de mesa basculante y explorará la posibilidad de una consulta con un especialista en disautonomía/POTS.
